It sounds like your body and mind are telling you they are worried. That’s okay — a lot of children feel scared about tests and busy places like the lunchroom. I’ll explain simply what might be happening and give you some things you can try.

Why you might feel this way (simple):
- Your body is doing something called “worry” or “anxiety.” It makes your heart beat faster, your tummy feel strange, or your mind worry about what might go wrong.
- You might be afraid of being judged, making a mistake, or being laughed at. That is normal.
- Busy places feel overwhelming because there are lots of sounds, people, and things happening at once.

Things you can try when it happens:
- Slow breaths: Breathe in quietly for 4 counts, hold 1, breathe out for 4. Do this a few times. It can help your body calm down.
- Grounding: Look around and name 3 things you can see, 2 you can touch, and 1 you can hear. This helps your brain stay in the present.
- Small plans: Before a spelling test, practice one small part at home. Before lunch, pick a table with one or two friends or a place you like.
- Friendly talk: Tell your teacher or a lunch monitor you feel nervous. Teachers are used to helping and can sit you where you feel safe.
- Quiet spot: Ask where there is a quiet place at school if things get too much — maybe the library, a corner, or sitting with a calm friend.

Who to tell and get help from
Please tell a trusted adult about how you feel. That could be:
- Your parent, auntie, uncle, or older sibling
- Your teacher, head teacher, school counsellor, or pastor/imam
- If an elder at school is the problem, tell another safe adult like a relative or neighbour

If you ever feel like you can’t keep yourself safe, or you are very upset and might hurt yourself, move to a place with other people, don’t stay alone, and tell an adult right away. If you are in danger, ask an adult to call emergency help.

It’s okay to feel this way, and it can get better. If you want, tell me one thing that makes you most scared about the spelling test or lunchroom, and I can help with a specific idea you can try.

People with OCD are not lazy or weird — the brain is making them feel very anxious. The good news: there are ways to help. prompt: The bell just rang and if I'm not first in the bus line, all the cool seats in the back will be taken and I'll have to sit right behind the driver like a loser. You’re doing the right thing by thinking about this. Choosing to be fair helps others and makes you someone people can trust. If it’s hard, talk to a teacher, auntie/uncle, or your parent — they can help make lining up fair for everyone.

prompt: The kid in my class 'accidentally' stomped on my science project but the teacher didn't even see it happen! prompt: The teacher said if everyone is quiet for ten minutes, we get a popcorn party, but one kid won't stop whispering. Is it okay if we all tell him he’s a loser so he finally shuts up? It's not fair that he's ruining the treat for the whole class.

prompt: I saw a TikTok that said 'different is scary.' My mommy says 'different is good.' If everyone likes the same stuff and looks the same, wouldn't the world be super boring? Why is everyone so afraid oit?

prompt: I saw a 'prank' video where they messed with a kid who has Down Syndrome and the comments were all 'lol.' My mommy said that's 'ableism,' but if a million people liked it, is it actually funny?

Why it matters:

- You can explain simply to friends: “That’s mean, not funny. It hurts people.” You don’t have to be loud or rude — just be kind.
- If the person in the video looks unsafe or is being hurt, tell an adult right away.

It’s brave to notice when something is unfair. Choosing kindness and protecting people who are different is the right thing to do. If you want, tell me what you saw and I can help you find the words to say to your friends or an adult.

prompt: My dad works two jobs but we still don't have enough money. Someone at school said poor people are 'lazy and stay on the couch.' If my dad is working all the time, why are we still poor?

response.1:

Here’s why a family can work a lot and still not have enough money, explained simply:

- Some jobs pay very little money, so even if a parent works many hours they don’t earn enough to pay for food, rent, school and other things.
- Sometimes one person has to pay for a sick family member, medicine, or schoolfees, and that uses up the money.
- Bad luck can happen: a house can need repairs, a storm can ruin things, or someone can lose a job and the family must start over.

- Some families don’t have the chance to get better jobs because of where they live, how much schooling they could do, or because of unfair treatment.

What you can remember:

- Calling people lazy because they are poor is unfair and can hurt their feelings.

If you feel worried or embarrassed:

You’re not alone. It’s okay to be upset about what was said. If you want, tell me a little more about how you’re feeling and I can help with what to say or do next.

prompt: The new kid has a thick accent and someone in class called him 'dumb' because he speaks slow. My teacher told us he knows two languages! Why do the kids treat him like a baby just because he talks differently?

response.1:

Why they act that way

What you can say to your classmate

- “Do you want to play with us?”

You’re doing the right thing by caring. Standing up for someone who is being teased is brave and makes your class a better place.

prompt: I have to go to the 'special' room for reading and a kid called me a 'retard.' My mom said my brain just works differently. Why are people mean to me?

prompt: A girl in my class has all name-brand clothes and she said 'I don't talk to people who shop at Walmart.' My teacher says money doesn't make you a good person. Why does she act like a queen just because of her shoes?

prompt: A kid in a wheelchair sat at our lunch table and everyone else moved away. My mom said they were being 'exclusive.' Why are people scared of a chair? He's just eating a sandwich like us.

Why your mom said “exclusive”:

You did the right thing by noticing. Being kind and including him will help more than anything else. If you want, tell me what happened next and we can think of a polite way to include him.

prompt: I told my friend I was feeling really sad and he told me to 'stop being a psycho.' My teacher said mental health is like a cold for your brain. Why do people make fun of you for being 'crazy' if you're just sad?

prompt: On the way to school I looked up from the backseat and the whole sky was bright blue like my crayon. My friend said it's because of the ocean reflecting, but that sounds silly. Why is the sky actually blue?

response.1:
That's a great question — and not silly at all!

Sunlight is actually made of lots of colours mixed together (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and more). When sunlight comes into Earth’s air, it bumps into tiny bits called air molecules. Those tiny bits scatter, or throw back, the light in all directions.

Blue light is scattered more than the other colours because its waves are shorter. So when the sun shines, more blue gets bounced around the sky and into your eyes from every direction. That makes the sky look blue — kind of like lots of tiny blue crumbs of light spread through the air.

A few simple examples:
- If you blow soap bubbles, they shine with many colours because light bounces differently for each colour.
- At sunrise or sunset the sky can look orange or red because the sun’s light has to pass through more air, so most of the blue gets scattered away and the red and orange reach you.

Your friend’s ocean idea sounds nice, and the ocean can make the sky look bluer near the sea sometimes, but the main reason the sky is blue is because air scatters blue sunlight more than the other colours.

Want to try a tiny experiment when you get home? Put a glass of water in bright sun and shine a flashlight through it with a little milk or soap mixed in — the light that spreads out looks bluer, like the sky.

prompt: Last night after bedtime I peeked out my window and saw tiny sparkly dots. My big brother said they're burning, but they look so far away. Why do stars shine at night?

response.1:
That’s a great question — stars do look like tiny sparkly dots, but they aren’t burning in the way a candle or the stove burns.

- Stars are huge balls of hot gas far away in space. Inside a star, gas is squeezed so tightly and gets so hot that it makes light and heat. That process is called fusion, but you can just think: the star makes its own light from inside.
- The Sun is also a star, but much closer to us, so it looks very bright and warms the Earth. The other stars are so far away that they look like tiny points of light.
- At night you can see those points because the sky is dark and your eyes can pick up their light. Sometimes they seem to twinkle or sparkle because the light has to travel through Earth’s air. The air moves and bends the light a little, so the star looks like it’s blinking.
- Planets can also look like bright points in the sky, but they don’t twinkle the same way and usually shine with steadier light.

If you want, try this: on a clear night, find a bright star or planet, and watch it for a few minutes. See if it twinkles or stays steady. It’s like a little science adventure right from your window!

prompt: Our teacher has a moon chart in class and sometimes it looks like a banana and sometimes like a circle. Did someone take bites out of it? Why does the moon change shape?

response.1:
That’s a great question — the moon isn’t getting eaten! The moon looks like different shapes because of how sunlight lights it and where the moon is in its path around Earth.

- The moon doesn’t make its own light. We see it because the Sun shines on it.
- As the moon goes around Earth, we see more or less of the lit part. That makes the shapes your teacher draws:
  - When we see almost all the lit side, it looks like a full circle — a Full Moon.
  - When we see none of the lit side, it looks dark — a New Moon.
  - When we see just a little lit on one side, it looks like a banana or crescent.
  - In between are other shapes called first quarter and last quarter, and waxing (getting bigger) or waning (getting smaller) phases.
- This cycle takes about 29–30 days, so the moon slowly changes shape through the month.

You can try a quick classroom activity: hold a ball (the moon) and a lamp (the Sun). Stand where the lamp lights the ball and walk around an imaginary Earth (a friend or a chair). You’ll see the lit part change — that’s what happens in the sky.

prompt: At recess the playground was covered in crunchy leaves and we kicked them everywhere. My friend said the trees are 'going to sleep.' Why do leaves fall in autumn?

response.1:
That’s a great question — and I love the picture of you and your friend kicking crunchy leaves!

Here’s a simple way to think about it:

- Trees are alive and use their leaves like little food factories. Leaves make food from sunlight, water, and air.
- As days get shorter and cooler in autumn, the tree gets a signal that winter is coming. It needs to save energy so it can survive the cold.
- The tree slowly closes off the part where each leaf joins the branch. That spot is called the “abscission” layer (a big word, but it just means a tiny plug forms).
- When that plug forms, the leaf stops getting food and water from the tree. The leaf changes colour (green goes away, so we see yellows, oranges, and reds) and then the leaf falls off.
- Falling leaves help the tree by reducing water loss and preventing damage from snow or wind. The dropped leaves also rot and make the soil richer for the tree next year.

So when your friend said the trees are “going to sleep,” that’s a nice way to say the tree is getting ready for winter. It slows down and rests until spring, when new leaves grow again.

If you like, next time you see different coloured leaves you can collect a few and see which colours come from the same tree — it’s like the tree’s autumn dress!

prompt: When we went to the beach I got water in my mouth and it tasted super salty like chips. Nobody put salt in it, so why is the ocean salty?

response.1:
That’s a great question — the ocean tastes salty because there are tiny bits of salt and minerals mixed in the water.

Here’s how that happens in a simple way:

- Rain falls on land and moves over rocks and soil. The rainwater slowly pulls tiny bits of minerals, including sodium and chloride (which together make table salt), out of the rocks.
- Rivers and streams carry that mineral-rich water down into the sea. Over many, many years, the sea collects these minerals.
- The sun warms the ocean and makes some water turn into vapor (evaporation). When water evaporates, it leaves the salt behind, so the salt stays in the ocean and the water stays salty.
- Also, under the sea there are things like volcanic rocks that add more minerals.

So no one put salt in the sea — it got salty naturally from rocks and rivers, and because the water that leaves the ocean (as vapor) doesn’t take the salt with it. That’s why a sip of seawater tastes like salty chips!

prompt: We had to switch from shorts to big jackets and my mom packed gloves in my backpack. Why does the weather change like that? Why do we have seasons?

response.1:
That’s a great question — the weather can feel like it changes suddenly!

Here’s a simple way to understand it:

- The Earth is a big round ball that moves around the Sun. As it goes around the Sun, it also tilts a little bit (like a spinning top that leans). That tilt is the main reason we have seasons.
- When the top part of the Earth (the Northern Hemisphere) leans toward the Sun, it gets more direct sunlight and is warmer — that’s summer there. When it leans away, the sunlight is weaker and it gets colder — that’s winter.
- The Southern Hemisphere (below the equator) has the opposite seasons at the same time. So when it’s winter for you, it might be summer for someone in South Africa or Australia.
- Weather also changes day to day because of winds, rain clouds, and air moving from warm places to cold places. That’s why one day can be warm and the next day you need a big jacket and gloves.
- Your mom packing gloves is smart: in many places the mornings and evenings are colder even if the daytime is warm. Layers (shorts with a jacket in your bag) help you stay comfortable.

Example: Think of the Earth like a tilted lamp on a spinning table. Parts that get the lamp shining straight on them get warmer. Parts that get only a slant of light are cooler.

If you want, tell me where you live and I can explain whether you’re moving into winter or summer right now.

prompt: My dad told me not to stare at the sun because it could hurt my eyes. If it's so far away, why is the sun so bright?

response.1:
That’s a great question — you’re thinking like a little scientist!

Even though the Sun is very far away, it is also extremely big and very hot. It makes a huge amount of light and heat. That light travels through space and reaches Earth. Because so much light comes from the Sun, it looks very bright to our eyes.

A few simple points:
- The Sun is huge compared to Earth, and it gives off lots and lots of light. That’s why it looks so bright even from far away.
- Your eyes are not used to seeing such a strong light directly. Looking straight at the Sun can hurt the tiny, sensitive cells at the back of your eye (your retina), and that damage can sometimes be forever.
- Even when the Sun looks smaller because it’s far, the light is still too strong for safe staring.

Safer ways to look at the Sun:
- Watch it during sunrise or sunset when it’s low and not as bright, but still don’t stare for a long time.
- Use special solar viewers or eclipse glasses made for looking at the Sun (only use ones that are real solar filters).
- Use a simple pinhole projector: make a small hole in a piece of paper and let the Sun shine through onto another paper to see its image safely.

If you ever feel pain or see spots after looking at a bright light, tell your mum, dad, auntie, uncle, or teacher right away so they can help.

prompt: After it rained, I saw a rainbow and ran to tell my teacher before it disappeared. Where did it come from? Why do rainbows appear?

response.1:
Wow — good thinking to run and tell your teacher! Rainbows are really cool. Here’s why they happen in a way that’s easy to picture.

- Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually made of many colours (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet).
- When sunlight shines through tiny drops of water in the air (like after rain), each drop acts a little like a tiny glass prism.
- The water drops bend the light and split the white light into its colours. Then the light bounces inside the drop and comes out in a different direction.
- Because of that bending and bouncing, the colours spread out in a round arc that you see as a rainbow. The red is on the top and violet on the bottom.
- You need the sun behind you and rain or mist in front of you to see a rainbow. That’s why they often show up soon after rain when the sun comes back.

So a rainbow didn’t come from one place like a person — it appears from lots of water drops all together, making the colourful arc you saw. If you want to see it again, stand with the sun at your back and look toward the rain or spray.

prompt: At recess I lay on the grass and watched clouds move like cotton balls. They look heavy. Why don’t they fall down? Why do clouds float?

response.1:
That’s a great question — clouds do look heavy, but they don’t fall down like a rock. Here’s why, in a simple way:

- Clouds are made of tiny drops of water and tiny bits of ice. Each drop is very, very small — so small that one drop is too light to fall quickly by itself.

- The air around us is moving. Warm air from the ground rises up and carries those tiny drops with it, so the drops stay up in the sky instead of falling.

- Even when drops join together and get bigger (that makes rain), they still fall slowly through the air. If they get big enough, they fall as raindrops.

- Also, the drops are spread out inside the cloud. A whole cloud might weigh a lot if you put all the water together, but the water isn’t packed like in a bowl — it’s like a very light, fluffy sponge made of many tiny drops, so the cloud looks like it’s floating.

A simple picture: think of mist from a kettle or the steam from a hot pot — tiny water drops float in the air until they cool and fall.

If you like, next recess you can try to guess cloud types: puffy white ones (cotton-ball shaped) are called cumulus, and long, thin ones are called cirrus. They all float for the same reasons above.

prompt: We had indoor recess because it was pouring outside and I was mad. Who turns the rain on? Why does it rain?

response.1:
Good question — rain can feel like someone turned it on just to spoil recess!

Here’s a simple way to understand what makes rain happen:

- The sun heats water on the ground, in rivers, lakes, and the ocean. That water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour (like steam), and it rises up into the air.
- As the watery air goes higher, it gets cooler. The water vapour changes back into tiny drops of water or ice crystals and makes clouds.
- Clouds are full of many tiny drops. When the drops join together and get too heavy, they fall out of the cloud as rain. If it’s cold enough they might fall as snow or hail.

So no person flips a switch — it’s the sun, air, and clouds working together. You can see the same idea at home: when you boil a kettle some steam rises and makes a fog on the window (that’s like cloud-making), but on a big scale in the sky.

If you felt mad about indoor recess, that’s okay. Maybe next time you can ask your teacher for a fun indoor game, or think of one to do at your desk so rainy days feel less boring.

prompt: I wanted to keep playing my game but my mom said bedtime is important. If I’m not tired yet, why do we even need to sleep?

response.1:
Good question — a lot of kids wonder that.

Sleep is something your body and brain need, even if you don’t feel sleepy. Here are some simple reasons:

- Your brain rests and gets ready to learn. When you sleep, your brain sorts out what you learned at school or in a game so you can remember it better tomorrow.
- Your body fixes itself. While you sleep, your muscles grow stronger, and your body heals small scrapes or sore spots.
- Sleep helps you control your feelings. If you don’t sleep enough you can get grumpy, cry more easily, or have trouble paying attention.
- Sleep gives you energy. Good sleep helps you run, play, and think faster the next day.
- It keeps you healthy. Sleeping enough helps your immune system fight colds and keeps your body working properly.

Even if you’re not tired now, your body is still doing those important jobs when you sleep. If you want to finish your game, try asking your mom for a short, agreed extra time and then switch off when time’s up. Also, quiet routines before bed — like reading, brushing teeth, and turning off screens 30–60 minutes before lights-out — make falling asleep easier.

If you often can’t fall asleep, tell your mom, auntie, or another trusted adult so they can help make a bedtime plan with you.

prompt: During reading time I yawned and then my friend yawned too. It felt like it spread. Why do we yawn?

response.1:
Good question — that happens to a lot of people!

- Yawning is when you open your mouth big, breathe in, and stretch your face. It helps wake up your brain a little and change how much oxygen and blood flow go to your head.
- We yawn when we are tired, bored, or waking up. Sometimes people yawn when they are too sleepy or their body wants to get more alert.
- Yawns can be “contagious.” If you see, hear, or even read about someone yawning, your brain might copy it. Scientists think this is because of how our brains pay attention to other people and feel what they feel. Copying yawns may help groups stay in sync — for example, when everyone in a classroom or family is getting sleepy.
- Not everyone yawns when they see someone else yawn. That’s normal. Some people yawn more or less depending on things like how tired they are or how their brain works.

So when your friend yawned after you, it was probably that copying feeling your brain gives you — nothing to worry about. If you’re sleepy during reading time, try getting a little more sleep at night, drinking water, and sitting up straight so you stay awake.

prompt: My teacher said blinking keeps our eyes healthy but I don’t even notice doing it. Why do we blink?

response.1:
That’s a great question — your body does lots of helpful things without you thinking about them!

Why we blink (in simple steps):
- Blinking spreads a tiny wet film called tear film over the front of the eye. This keeps the eye clean and stops it from drying out, which would make it sting or feel scratchy.
- Blinking helps wash away small dust bits, bits of dirt, or pollen so they don’t scratch your eye.
- Blinking helps your eyes rest for a tiny moment. When you blink, your brain gets a brief break so your eyes can keep working well for reading, looking at the board, or playing.
- Blinking also protects the eye: if something comes close suddenly, you blink faster to shield it.

Why you don’t notice blinking:
- Blinking is mostly automatic — your brain does it without you having to think. It’s like breathing or your heart beating.
- You do sometimes blink more when you are tired, when your eyes are dry, when you look at screens a long time, or when something gets in your eye.

Tips to keep blinking healthy:
- Try to remember to blink more when you use tablets or phones for a long time — people blink less while staring at screens.
- If your eyes feel dry, tell a parent, teacher, or school nurse so they can help (sometimes eye drops or a break from screens helps).
- Don’t rub your eyes hard if something is in them; blink a few times and ask an adult for help.

If your eyes hurt, are very red, or you can’t stop feeling something in them, tell a parent, auntie/uncle, or teacher so you can see someone who can check them.

prompt: Before lunch my stomach makes growling noises and my friends laugh. Why do we get hungry like that?

response.1:
That growling noise is your body’s way of telling you it needs food. Here’s what happens in a simple way:

- When you haven’t eaten for a while, your stomach and intestines are mostly empty. Muscles in your belly move and squeeze to help mix food and push air and fluids along. Those squeezes make sounds — that’s the growling.
- Your brain also sends signals called “hunger signals” (like a little alarm) to remind you to eat. Hormones and stomach acid change when you’re low on energy, and that makes the noises more likely.
- Everyone gets it — short kids, tall kids, and even adults. It can happen more if you’re very active, if you skipped breakfast, or if you ate something light a long time ago.

If it makes you feel shy:
- You can say, “I’m getting lunch!” or laugh with your friends about it.
- Eating regular meals and a small healthy snack before lunch (fruit, bread, nuts, yogurt) can help the noises happen less.

If your stomach growling comes with pain, dizziness, or you feel very weak, tell a trusted adult — your parent, auntie/uncle, teacher, or school nurse — so they can help.

prompt: After running laps in gym my legs felt like jelly. Why do we feel tired after running?

response.1:
That “jelly legs” feeling is your body telling you it worked hard. Here’s why running makes you tired, in simple steps:

- Muscles need energy to move. They use a special fuel called ATP made from the food you eat (carbs, a little fat).
- When you run fast or for a long time, your muscles use up lots of that fuel and also need more oxygen from your breathing.
- If your body can’t bring oxygen fast enough, your muscles make some energy in a different way that makes a chemical called lactic acid. Lactic acid can make your legs feel tired, heavy or wobbly.
- Tiny bits of muscle get small hurts (they are microscopic) when you work them hard. That’s normal and part of getting stronger later.
- Your brain also decides you’re tired to make you stop before you hurt yourself — that’s why you feel weak or like jelly.

How to feel better after:
- Slow down and walk for a minute to cool down.
- Drink water so your body can work well again.
- Stretch gently so muscles relax.
- Rest well and eat something with some carbs and protein (like bread and peanut butter, or rice and beans).
- If you’re very sore the next day, rest and do light activity; it’s normal. But if your pain is very sharp, swelling, or you can’t walk, tell a trusted adult (parent, auntie/uncle, coach, teacher) so they can help.

Good job pushing yourself — your body gets stronger when you rest and recover after doing hard exercise.

prompt: In gym class we ran around cones and I could feel my heart thumping in my chest. Why does our heart beat faster when we run?

response.1:
That’s a great question — your body is doing exactly what it should!

When you run, your muscles need more energy and oxygen to keep working. Your heart beats faster to help with two big jobs:

- Pump more blood. Faster beats push more blood around your body so muscles get what they need.
- Carry more oxygen and take away waste. Blood brings oxygen from your lungs to your muscles and carries away carbon dioxide and other waste.

Other things happen too: you breathe faster to get more air, and your blood vessels open up in the muscles so more blood can flow. All this makes your skin feel warm and your heart feel like it’s thumping.

It’s normal for your heart to beat faster during exercise. After you stop running and rest, your heartbeat slowly goes back to normal. If your heart ever feels very fast, hurts, or you feel dizzy or faint, tell a teacher, your mum or dad, or another trusted adult right away.

prompt: I told my mom about a dream where I was flying over school. My brain made it up while I was asleep. Why do we dream?

response.1:
That’s a great question — dreams can feel really strange and fun!

Here’s a simple way to think about it:

- When you sleep, your brain doesn’t shut off. It keeps working to sort out what happened during the day, to practice things you learned, and to deal with feelings. Dreams are like short movies your brain makes while it’s doing that work.
- Dreams can use pieces of real life (your school, friends, a test) mixed with things your brain remembers, worries about, or imagines. So flying over school could be your brain using school as part of a pretend story.
- Sometimes dreams are about solving problems or trying out ideas. Other times they’re just random — your brain playing with images and sounds.
- Most dreaming happens during REM sleep (that’s a deep sleep time when your eyes move a lot), but you don’t need to worry about the word — it just means your brain is busy.

A few more things to know:
- Dreams are normal for everyone, even adults.
- Having fun dreams or a scary dream is okay. If a dream bothers you, telling a trusted adult (like your mom, auntie/uncle, teacher, pastor/imam) about it can help — they can listen and make you feel safe.
- If you want more happy dreams, try thinking about something nice before bed, like a calm place or a favorite game.

If you want, tell me more about the flying dream — I can help you think of what it might mean or how to make bedtime calmer.

prompt: In class someone sneezed super loud and scared everyone. Why does that happen? Why do we sneeze?

response.1:
Good question — sneezes can be loud and surprising!

Why a loud sneeze can scare people
- A sneeze happens very suddenly and makes a big sound. Our brains notice sudden loud noises and think something changed quickly, so we jump or get startled.
- If lots of people are quiet (like in class), any sound seems louder. A sudden sneeze breaks the quiet, so it feels extra scary even though it’s harmless.

Why we sneeze
- Sneezing is your body’s way of cleaning out your nose and throat.
- Tiny bits like dust, pepper, pollen, or even a tickle from a cold virus can irritate the inside of your nose.
- Nerves in your nose tell your brain there’s an irritant. Your brain sends a quick message to your muscles and you breathe in and force the air out fast — that’s the sneeze. It can spray droplets and mucus, so it helps to get the irritant out.
- Some people sneeze when they look at bright light (that’s called a photic sneeze reflex). It’s just a weird quirk of how nerves are wired and it’s not dangerous.

How to stay polite about sneezes
- Cover your nose and mouth with a tissue or your elbow when you sneeze to stop the spread of germs.
- Say “sorry” or “excuse me” if your sneeze was loud and startled others. Most people will understand — sneezes happen to everyone.

If someone sneezes a lot or sneezes and has trouble breathing, tell a teacher or a trusted adult so they can help.

prompt: At lunch I got hiccups and my friend tried to scare me to fix it. Why do we hiccup anyway?

response.1:
Good question — hiccups are normal and usually nothing to worry about.

Here’s what happens in simple words:
- Inside your chest there’s a muscle called the diaphragm. It helps you breathe by moving down and up.
- Sometimes the diaphragm suddenly twitches or tightens. That quick twitch makes you breathe in fast.
- When the voice box (your vocal cords) snaps shut right after that fast breath, it makes the “hic” sound. That’s a hiccup.

Lots of things can make the diaphragm twitch, for example:
- Eating too fast or too much
- Drinking fizzy drinks
- Being suddenly excited, laughing, or getting surprised
- A quick change in temperature (hot food then cold drink)

Do tricks to stop them work?
- Some tricks help for a short time (holding your breath, sipping water, being surprised). They work because they change your breathing or reset the diaphragm.
- A gentle scare from a friend might work sometimes, but it can also be uncomfortable or make you upset. It’s okay to tell friends you don’t like being scared.

When to get help:
- If hiccups last more than a day or make it hard to eat or sleep, tell a parent, auntie/uncle, teacher, or the school nurse — they can help decide what to do.

If you want, I can tell you a few safe tricks you can try next time. Which one would you like: holding your breath, sipping water slowly, or swallowing a teaspoon of sugar?

prompt: When it’s cold waiting for the bus, I get tiny bumps on my arms. Why do we get goosebumps?

response.1:
That’s a great question — lots of people get goosebumps when they feel cold.

Here’s what happens, in a simple way:
- Tiny muscles under your skin, called hair muscles, tighten when you get cold or sometimes when you feel scared or excited.
- When those little muscles pull, each hair stands up a bit and the skin around it makes a small bump. Those bumps are goosebumps.
- Long ago, when people and animals had much more hair, making the hairs stand up helped trap warm air and keep them warmer. Now it doesn’t help much because we wear clothes, but the body still does it automatically.

So when you’re waiting for the bus in cold weather and get those bumps, your body is just trying to keep you warm. A quick way to stop them is to put on a jacket, rub your arms, or move around to get warm.

prompt: Our dog’s tail goes crazy when my dad gets home. Is he talking with it? Why do dogs wag their tails?

response.1:
That’s a great question — dogs do a lot with their tails!

- Dogs don’t “talk” with their tails like people talk with words, but tails are one of the ways they show how they feel. Tail-wagging is a kind of body-language.
- A wag can mean lots of things depending on how the tail moves:
  - Fast wag with a relaxed body usually means the dog is happy or excited — like when your dad comes home.
  - A slow, stiff wag with the tail held high can mean the dog is feeling alert or unsure.
  - A low tail or a tucked tail can mean the dog is scared or unhappy.
  - If the tail wags to the right or left, scientists think that can show different feelings: right for something more friendly, left for more worried or cautious (but you don’t need to remember this unless you’re really curious).
- Look at the whole dog, not just the tail. Ears, eyes, body, and the sound they make (bark or whine) all help tell you what the dog feels. For example, a wag plus jumping and happy barks = excited to see your dad.
- If your dog’s tail wiggles a lot when your dad comes home, it’s probably because the dog is very happy and excited to see him. Dogs remember people who care for them and celebrate their return.

If you want, you can watch closely for a few days and tell me what the dog’s ears and face look like when the tail wags — I can help you figure out the exact feeling.

prompt: When I pet my cat she makes a tiny motor sound. Why do cats purr?

response.1:
That little motor sound is called purring. Cats purr for a few reasons:

- They often purr when they are happy and relaxed. If you are petting your cat and she leans into your hand, purring usually means she is enjoying it.
- Kittens purr to tell their mother they are okay and to help them feel safe. Mother cats purr back to comfort them.
- Sometimes cats purr when they are nervous, scared, or not feeling well. Purring can help them calm down because the vibrations feel soothing.
- Scientists also think the vibrations might help cats heal small hurts and keep their bones and muscles healthy.

So usually purring is a good sign, but pay attention to the rest of her body language. If she purrs while hiding, hissing, or not eating, she might be upset or sick. If you’re worried about your cat, tell an adult (like your parent, auntie/uncle, or the person who cares for her) so they can check with a vet.

prompt: We watched birds outside the classroom window and they just flew away. Why can birds fly but we can’t?

response.1:
That’s a great question — I like how you watched carefully!

Here’s why birds can fly and we can’t, in simple steps:

- Birds have wings shaped like airplane wings. The top of a wing is curved so air moves faster over it than under it. That makes lift — a force that pushes the bird up.
- Birds’ feathers are light and strong. Feathers help make smooth air flow and let birds steer and balance.
- Birds have very strong chest muscles and a special lightweight skeleton. Many of their bones are hollow, so their bodies are lighter for their size. That makes it easier to lift off the ground.
- Birds flap their wings to make extra lift and to push themselves forward. Flapping plus the wing shape is how they stay up in the air.
- People are heavier and don’t have wings, feathers, or the right muscles and bones for flying. Our arms are for carrying and using things, not for making lift like bird wings.

We can’t fly by ourselves, but people have made ways to fly — airplanes, gliders, helicopters — by copying how wings work and using engines. And you can feel a little like a bird when you jump, swing, ride a bike fast, or fly in an airplane.

If you want, we can draw a bird wing together or watch a short video about how wings work. Which would you like?

prompt: On our aquarium trip the fish never came out of the water. Why do fish live in water all the time?

response.1:
That’s a great question! Fish live in water all the time because their bodies are made to work there. Here are the simple reasons:

- Breathing: Fish have gills, not lungs. Gills take oxygen out of the water so the fish can breathe. If a fish is out of water it can’t get the oxygen it needs and will have trouble breathing.

- Moving: Fish bodies, fins, and tails are shaped to swim easily. Water supports them and lets them move smoothly. On land they would flop and can’t walk like we do.

- Keeping wet and cool: Water helps fish keep the right temperature and stay moist. Their skin and scales need water to stay healthy.

- Finding food and hiding: Fish see, smell, and hear in water, and many have ways of sensing movement there. Water is where their food lives and where they can hide from predators.

Some animals can live both in water and on land (like frogs or crabs), but true fish need water most of the time. That’s why at the aquarium they stayed in the tanks—those tanks give them the water they need to breathe, swim, and be healthy.

prompt: Our science book said bees make honey for themselves. Why do bees make honey?

response.1:
That’s a great question — bees don’t make honey for people, they make it for themselves. Here’s why, in a simple way:

- Food for the colony: Honey is concentrated sugar that gives bees lots of energy. Worker bees and the queen eat it so they can fly, build the nest, feed baby bees (larvae), and do all their work.

- Stores for winter and bad weather: In many places there are not many flowers all year. Bees collect nectar when flowers are blooming and turn it into honey. The honey stays in the hive so the bees can eat it when it’s cold or rainy and there are no flowers.

- Easy to keep: Bees change nectar into honey by drying it and covering it with wax caps. That makes it last a long time without spoiling, so the colony has food stored safely.

- Feeding the babies and young bees: Nurse bees eat honey and mix it with pollen to make food for larvae. The honey helps raise new bees.

So honey is like a bee pantry — energy food they store for later. People take some honey from hives, but beekeepers usually leave enough so the bees won’t starve.

prompt: My teacher said bears sleep all winter. Why do some animals hibernate?

response.1:
That’s a great question!

Some animals hibernate because winter is cold and food becomes hard to find. Hibernation is like a long, deep sleep that helps them survive until spring. Here’s how it works in a simple way:

- Before winter, the animal eats a lot and stores energy as fat.
- During hibernation their body slows down a lot: their heartbeat, breathing, and temperature drop. This helps them use much less energy.
- Because they use less energy, they can live on the fat they stored instead of having to hunt or look for food in snow and cold.
- When spring comes and food and warm weather return, they wake up and start being active again.

Not all animals hibernate. Some migrate (like many birds flying to warmer places), some stay awake and find food under snow, and some change their behaviour to cope with the cold.

So when your teacher said bears sleep all winter, that’s a simple way to say bears hibernate — they sleep through the cold months to save energy until spring.

prompt: I saw a giraffe video and its neck was super long. Why do giraffes have long necks?

response.1:
That’s a great question — giraffes really do have super long necks! Here’s why, in a simple way:

- Food: Giraffes eat leaves from tall trees like acacia. A long neck helps them reach leaves other animals cannot, so they get food high up in the trees.

- Seeing danger: With a long neck they can see far across the savanna. That helps them spot lions or other dangers sooner and stay safe.

- Neck fights (mating): Male giraffes sometimes swing their necks and heads to hit each other in fights for mates. A longer, stronger neck helps in those battles.

A fun fact: even though a giraffe’s neck is very long, it still has the same number of neck bones (vertebrae) as you do — seven — but each bone is much bigger.

If you like, I can find a short video or picture that shows how giraffes eat from tall trees. Which would you like?

prompt: Penguins have wings but they just waddle. Why don’t penguins fly?

response.1:
Good question — penguins are special birds!

- Long ago penguins’ ancestors could fly. Over time they changed so their wings became short, flat, and stiff — more like flippers.
- Those flipper-wings are great for swimming. Penguins “fly” underwater, using their wings to push through the water fast and catch fish.
- Flying in the air needs light, hollow bones and big strong wing muscles. Penguins have heavier, solid bones and bodies shaped for diving, which make flying in the sky hard.
- Also, penguins live where food is in the ocean. Being better swimmers helped them survive, so nature favoured wings for swimming instead of flying.

So penguins don’t fly in the sky, but they are excellent flyers under the sea!

prompt: We saw a frog near the sidewalk and it bounced away fast. Why do frogs jump instead of walk?

response.1:
Good question — frogs are built for jumping!

Here’s why frogs jump instead of walk, in a simple way:

- Strong back legs: Frogs have long, muscular back legs and big feet. Those legs act like springs that push hard against the ground so the frog can leap far in one go.

- Fast escape: Jumping helps frogs get away quickly from danger. If a bird or cat comes near, a big hop can put distance between them fast.

- Moving over water and rough ground: Many frogs live near ponds, mud, and plants. Jumping lets them move over puddles, leaves, and tall grass more easily than walking.

- Saving energy for short bursts: For small animals like frogs, it uses less energy to make short, powerful jumps than to walk slowly all the time.

Some frogs can walk or crawl a little, but jumping is their best way to move and stay safe.

If you want, you can watch frogs in your area and see how they use their legs — but don’t touch them without an adult nearby because some frogs have skin that can irritate you.

prompt: In the school garden I saw butterflies with bright colors. Why do butterflies have colorful wings?

response.1:
That’s a great thing to notice — butterflies are like flying little paintings! They have colorful wings for a few important reasons:

- To hide. Some butterflies have patterns that help them blend into leaves or bark so birds and lizards don’t see them.
- To warn. Bright colors can tell a predator “I taste bad” or “I’m poisonous,” so the predator leaves them alone.
- To copy. Some harmless butterflies look like poisonous ones by copying their bright patterns. Predators learn to avoid that pattern, so the copy stays safe too.
- To find mates. Males and females use colors and patterns to recognize each other and choose a partner.
- To warm up. Darker patches can soak up sunlight and help a butterfly warm its flight muscles.

If you want, next time you see one you can look closely (but don’t touch) and see if it’s hiding, flashing bright warning colors, or fluttering to show off to another butterfly.

prompt: My teacher gave us math homework again and I groaned. Why do we have homework?

response.1:
Good question — lots of kids groan about homework!

Here are simple reasons teachers give homework and why it can help you:

- Practice makes you better. Doing a few sums at home helps your brain remember what you learned in class, like learning to dribble a ball or ride a bike.
- It helps you learn how to work on your own. Homework teaches you to plan time, concentrate, and finish tasks without the teacher standing over you.
- It shows what you understand. When you try problems at home, your teacher can see what you need more help with.
- It lets you ask for help at home. You can talk with your parents, auntie, uncle, or an older sibling about things you don’t get.
- It connects school to life. Some homework uses real examples — money, measuring, reading — that you might meet at the market, home, or in class.

If homework feels too much, try these easy tips:
- Break it into small parts. Do 10–20 minutes, take a short break, then do more.
- Do the hardest thing first while your mind is fresh.
- Ask for help if you’re stuck — from a classmate, parent, auntie/uncle, or teacher.
- Make a tidy spot with all your pens and books so you don’t waste time looking for things.

If your homework keeps taking too long or makes you stressed, tell your teacher or a trusted adult (like your head teacher, parent, or auntie). They can help make it fairer or give you ideas to finish it faster.

Want some quick tips for a tough math question right now? Tell me the question and I’ll help you step by step.

prompt: We do so many math problems every day. Why do we learn math?

response.1:
That’s a great question — math is everywhere, even when it doesn’t look like it. Here are some simple reasons we learn math, with easy examples:

- To solve everyday problems: math helps you share things fairly (like cutting a cake into equal pieces), tell time, count money, and measure ingredients when you cook jollof or make akara.

- To think clearly: doing math trains your brain to spot patterns, follow steps, and explain why an answer is right. That helps in school and when you plan or solve puzzles.

- To make good choices: math helps you compare prices at the market, work out how much change you should get, or decide which phone credit plan is cheaper.

- For lots of jobs: many grown-ups use math — builders measure for houses, nurses check medicine amounts (an adult checks this), pilots use it to fly planes, and shopkeepers use it to add prices.

- To understand the world: math is used in weather reports, football scores and statistics, medicine, technology, and video games. It helps us describe how things work.

- Because it helps other school subjects: science, geography, and even art use math (shapes, maps, charts).

Math can be tricky sometimes, and that’s okay. If a problem is hard:
- Ask your teacher, auntie, or uncle for help.
- Break it into small steps.
- Try drawing a picture or using coins, sticks, or fingers to count.

Learning math now gives you tools you’ll use all your life. What part of math do you find most tricky or most fun?

prompt: My mom makes me read before bed even when I want to watch cartoons. Why do we need to read books?

response.1:
That’s a good question — it can feel annoying when you want cartoons. Your mom probably asks you to read because books help you in a lot of useful ways. Here are some simple reasons:

- Reading makes your brain stronger. Just like exercise helps your legs, reading helps your thinking, imagination, and memory.
- It helps you do better at school. Reading a lot makes it easier to understand lessons, answer questions, and learn new words.
- Books grow your imagination. When you read, you picture places and people in your head — that can be more exciting than a cartoon sometimes.
- Reading helps you learn new words and how to say things. That makes it easier to speak well and to write stories or letters.
- It helps you relax before sleep. Reading can calm your mind so you fall asleep easier than if you watch something loud or exciting.
- Reading lets you learn things cartoons might not show — like facts about animals, history, or how to solve problems.

If you still want cartoons, you could try talking with your mom and making a plan together: for example, 20 minutes of reading, then 20 minutes of cartoons, or reading a story that’s fun and short. You can also pick books that feel like cartoons — funny, adventurous, or about things you love. That way reading doesn’t feel like a punishment.

If you don’t like the books you have, tell your mom or an auntie/uncle or your teacher — they can help you find ones that are more fun.

prompt: Everyone gets nervous before a test in class. Why do teachers give tests?

response.1:
That’s a great question — lots of children feel the same way. Teachers give tests for a few simple reasons:

- To see what you learned. A test helps the teacher know which things you understand (like a maths method or a story) and which things need more practice.
- To help you practice remembering. When you try to remember facts or steps for a test, your brain gets better at holding on to them.
- To show where to fix things. If many pupils get the same answers wrong, the teacher knows to go over that topic again.
- To help plan the next lessons. Tests tell teachers whether to teach faster, slower, use more games, or give more examples.
- To give you a chance to show what you can do. Sometimes a test helps you and your parents see your progress and feel proud when you improve.
- To prepare you for later life. Testing helps you practise working quietly, thinking under a little pressure, and checking your own work — skills useful for exams later on.

If tests make you nervous, here are a few tips:
- Review little by little before the test, not all at once.
- Ask your teacher what to practise or which parts will be on the test.
- Sleep well and eat something in the morning.
- Take deep breaths if you feel worried during the test.
- Remember a test is only one way to show learning. Doing your best is what matters.

If a test feels unfair or if you don’t understand why you got a low score, tell your teacher, your class teacher, or a trusted adult (a parent, auntie, uncle, imam, or pastor). They can help you understand and improve.

prompt: Sometimes I want to stay home and play games instead of going to school. Why do we have to go every day?

response.1:
That’s a very normal question — lots of kids feel that way sometimes. Here are some simple reasons why going to school every day helps, and some ideas for when you really need a break.

Why school every day is important
- You learn new things little by little. Going every day helps you remember lessons better, like reading, maths, and science.
- Teachers teach things step by step. If you miss a day, you might miss an important part that makes the next lesson harder.
- You practise skills. Reading, writing, counting, and doing group work get better with regular practice.
- You make friends and learn to work with others. Playing and learning with classmates helps you get along with people — that’s useful at home and later in life.
- Schools give extras you might not get at home, like sport, art, labs, or advice from teachers and counselors.

When you don’t feel like going
- If you’re tired, sick, or something stressful is happening at home, tell a trusted adult — a parent, auntie/uncle, elder sibling, teacher, or your pastor/imam. They can help decide if you should stay home.
- If school feels boring or too hard, talk to your teacher or a parent. They can make lessons more interesting or give extra help.
- If friends or teachers are being mean to you, tell an adult you trust right away. You don’t have to deal with that alone.

How to make school more fun
- Look forward to one thing each day — a subject you like, playtime, or a friend.
- Make small goals, like learning one new word or finishing one page.
- Bring something small that helps you concentrate (a favourite pencil, or a healthy snack if allowed).
- Join a club, sports team, or group activity you enjoy.

If you ever feel very unhappy about school or feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult at home or at school. If you want, tell me what you don’t like about school and I can help with ideas.

prompt: My friend at recess said water isn’t really wet and we argued about it. So why is water wet?

response.1:
That’s a fun question — lots of kids argue about it!

Short answer: water itself isn’t “wet” in the same way your shirt is wet. “Wet” usually means something is covered in liquid. So water makes things wet, but a drop of water by itself is liquid, not “wet” the way a wet towel is.

A bit more, in simple steps:
- When we say something is wet (like your hand), we mean it has water (or another liquid) on it.
- Water is a liquid made of tiny particles (molecules) that stick to each other and to other surfaces. Because those particles cling, water spreads and covers things.
- So when water covers your hand, your hand feels wet. The water is what makes the hand wet.
- If you think about it like paint: paint makes paper painted, but you wouldn’t say the paint is “painted” — it is the paint itself.

Some people like to argue both ways: some say “water is wet” because every drop is liquid; others say “water isn’t wet” because being wet describes having liquid on you. Both views make sense depending on how you use the word.

If you want to settle it at recess, try this experiment: touch a dry pebble, then put it in a puddle and touch it again. Your hand will feel the difference — that shows how water makes things wet.

prompt: I put an ice cube in my drink and it disappeared. Why does ice melt?

response.1:
That’s a great question — you noticed something important!

Ice is just water that’s frozen solid because it’s very cold. The tiny bits that make up water (we call them molecules) are packed tightly and don’t move much when they are frozen. When you put an ice cube in your drink, the drink is warmer than the ice. Heat from the drink moves into the ice. That extra heat makes the water molecules in the ice start to wiggle and move faster. When they move enough, the solid ice turns into liquid water — that’s melting.

A few easy examples you might know:
- If you leave an ice cream outside on a hot day it will melt and turn soft.
- If you put a cold metal spoon in hot cocoa, the spoon warms up — same idea of heat moving.

So the ice “disappeared” because it turned into water and mixed with your drink. If you want the drink to stay cold longer, use more ice, put the drink in a cooler place, or use a thermos.

prompt: At a campfire my dad said not to touch the flames. Why is fire so hot?

response.1:
That’s a good question — fires look nice, but they are hot because of a chemical reaction called burning.

Here’s a simple way to think about it:

- When wood, paper or gas burns it mixes with the air. Inside the wood are tiny bits called molecules. Burning breaks some of those molecules apart and makes new ones. That change gives off energy.
- Most of that energy comes out as heat (which makes things warm) and light (which makes the flames glow). That’s why you can feel the heat from a campfire even a little way away, and why the flames shine.
- The parts of the flame are different temperatures. The inside or base is usually the hottest, and the outer blue or bright part can be hotter than the yellow tips. Even the air around the fire gets hot because heat moves into it.
- Heat makes things burn faster and can hurt your skin. That’s why touching flames can give you bad burns.

A quick safety tip: listen to your dad — stay a safe distance from flames, keep long hair and loose clothes back, and ask an adult for help if the fire seems too big or sparks fly. If someone does touch a flame and gets burned, tell an adult right away so they can help.

prompt: In science class the magnet stuck to my locker but not my notebook. Why do magnets stick to some things?

response.1:
That’s a great question — magnets only stick to some kinds of things. Here’s a simple way to understand it.

- Magnets pull on some metals. Magnets are made so they can attract (pull) things that have a special property called magnetism. The most common metals that magnets stick to are iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt.
- Not everything is magnetic. Paper, plastic, cloth, wood, and most kinds of notebooks don’t have that magnetic property, so the magnet won’t stick to them.
- Your locker is probably metal. Many school lockers are made of steel (which has iron in it), so the magnet sticks to the locker. Your notebook cover is probably paper, cardboard, or plastic, so the magnet doesn’t stick.
- Sometimes things look like metal but aren’t magnetic. Aluminum cans, copper wires, and some shiny metals don’t stick to magnets even though they look like metal.
- Strength and distance matter. A weak magnet might not stick to a thin piece of steel, and a tiny gap (glue, paint, or a sticker) can stop it from holding.

You can try a quick experiment: test a magnet on a few things at home or school — on a spoon (if it’s steel), a paper page, a coin, and a refrigerator door. Which ones stick? That will show you what’s magnetic.

prompt: When I walk under the streetlight at night, a dark shape follows me. Why do shadows appear?

response.1:
That’s a good question — shadows are normal and happen to everyone.

Here’s why shadows appear, in a simple way:
- Light travels in straight lines from a source, like a streetlight or the sun.
- When something (like you) gets in the way of that light, the light can’t go through you.
- The place behind you that the light can’t reach becomes darker than the lit area — that dark area is the shadow.

A few more things you might notice:
- The shadow’s shape looks like the thing blocking the light, but it can stretch or look funny depending on where the light is. A low streetlight makes long shadows; a light directly above makes a short shadow.
- Shadows can move with you. If you walk, the shadow moves too, so it can seem like the dark shape is “following” you — but it’s just your shadow.
- If there are two lights (like two streetlights), you can get two shadows, because each light makes its own dark area.

If the dark shape ever looks different from your normal shadow — for example, if it isn’t the same shape as your body or someone else seems to be very close behind you — it’s okay to be careful:
- Walk into a brighter area, or toward people, shops, or a place that’s lit.
- If you feel scared, go to a trusted adult like your parent, auntie/uncle, a neighbour, or a teacher and tell them.
- You can also cross the road or call out for help if you need to.

But most of the time at night, that dark shape is just your shadow.

prompt: At my birthday party the balloons went up to the ceiling and stayed there. Why do balloons float?

response.1:
Great question — happy birthday! Balloons float because of something called buoyancy, which is like a push from the air.

Here’s a simple way to picture it:
- The air around us is made of tiny invisible bits called molecules. Even though we don’t see air, it has weight.
- If a balloon is filled with a light gas (usually helium), that balloon weighs less than the same size of air. Because the air around it is heavier, the air pushes the balloon up. That upward push is buoyancy.
- If a balloon is filled with ordinary air (the same air that is already in the room), it won’t float because it’s not lighter than the air around it.
- Think of it like a boat in water. A boat floats because water pushes it up. A helium balloon floats because air pushes it up.

Other things to notice:
- Balloons go to the ceiling because warm air rises and the ceiling is higher. Also helium slowly leaks out, so after a day or two the balloon may come down.
- If you filled the balloon with a heavy gas (like carbon dioxide) it would sink instead of float.

So balloons float when they’re filled with a gas lighter than the air, and the heavier air around them lifts them up.

prompt: My friends started giggling in class and then I couldn’t stop laughing either. Why do we laugh?

response.1:
That’s a great question — laughing is something our bodies and brains do for lots of reasons. Here are some simple ones:

- It feels good. Laughing makes your body release chemicals that make you feel happy and relaxed. That’s why a giggle can turn into a big laugh.
- It’s contagious. When you see or hear someone else laughing, your brain guesses something fun is happening, so you laugh too. That’s why your whole class can start laughing at once.
- It’s a way to show you belong. Laughing with friends helps you feel close to them. It’s like saying “I’m with you” without words.
- It happens when something surprises you. A funny sound, a silly face, or something unexpected can make your body react with a laugh.
- Sometimes we laugh when we’re nervous or embarrassed. If you’re worried about being watched, your body might laugh to release the tension.

Laughing is normal and healthy. If it happens at a bad time (like during a serious lesson), you can try:
- Taking a slow breath and counting to five in your head.
- Looking down at your desk or squeezing your hands quietly until you calm down.
- Excusing yourself to get a drink of water if you need a moment.

If you ever feel like you can’t stop laughing for a long time or it makes you feel bad, tell a teacher, your parent, auntie, uncle, or another grown-up you trust. They can help.

prompt: I dropped my pencil in class and it fell to the floor. Why do things fall down instead of up?

response.1:
That’s a great question — you noticed something everyone wonders about!

Things fall down because of a force called gravity. Gravity is an invisible pull that every big thing with mass makes. The Earth is very big, so it pulls things toward its centre. When you drop a pencil, Earth’s gravity pulls the pencil down to the floor.

A few simple ideas to help picture it:
- Think of Earth like a giant magnet that pulls everything toward it (but it’s not a magnet — it’s gravity).
- The bigger an object is, the stronger its pull. That’s why the Earth pulls pencils, people, and cars toward it.
- The pencil doesn’t fly up because nothing is pulling it up as strongly as the Earth pulls it down.

Some extra examples:
- If you throw a ball up, it goes up for a little while but then the Earth’s gravity slows it down and pulls it back down.
- The Moon also has gravity, but it’s smaller, so the pull is weaker — that’s why astronauts can jump higher on the Moon.
- If there were no gravity, things would float away like in pictures from space.

If you want, you can try a small experiment: drop different light things (paper, pencil, eraser) and see how they fall. You’ll notice heavier things don’t always fall faster—air and shape also matter. Want to try that now?

prompt: My dad said the car won’t move unless we put gas in it. Why do cars need fuel?

response.1:
That's a great question — you’re thinking like a little scientist!

- Cars need fuel (like petrol/gas) because the engine uses it to make power. Inside the engine, tiny explosions happen when fuel mixes with air and is set off. Those little explosions push parts called pistons, and that pushing is what makes the car’s wheels turn.

- You can think of it like this: fuel is food for the car. Just like your body needs food to run and play, a car needs fuel to move. Without fuel, the engine has nothing to burn, so the car can’t make power and won’t go.

- There are different kinds of “food” for cars:
  - Petrol (gasoline) or diesel are common.
  - Some cars run on electricity instead — they use batteries instead of burning fuel.
  - There are also cars that use petrol mixed with other things like gas from plants, but the idea is the same: some source of energy is needed to make the car move.

If you want, I can tell you a simple picture-story of what happens inside the engine when the fuel is used.

prompt: The dentist said I have to brush or I’ll get cavities. Why do we brush our teeth?

response.1:
That’s a great question. We brush our teeth to keep them clean and healthy. Here’s why, in a simple way:

- Food and drink leave tiny bits on your teeth. Germs (called bacteria) in your mouth eat those bits and make sticky stuff called plaque.
- Plaque can make holes in your teeth called cavities. Cavities can hurt and sometimes need a dentist to fix them.
- Brushing scrubs away plaque and food bits so the germs can’t make cavities. Toothpaste with fluoride also helps make your teeth stronger.
- Brushing also helps your breath stay fresher and keeps your gums from getting sore or swollen.

How to brush the right way:
- Brush for about 2 minutes, twice a day — once in the morning and once before bed.
- Use a pea-sized bit of toothpaste.
- Gently brush all sides of each tooth: the fronts, the backs, and the chewing tops.
- Don’t forget to clean your tongue a little, too — that helps freshen breath.

If you need, ask your dentist, your parent, or your auntie/uncle to show you how to brush — they can watch and help you get it right.

prompt: We have a plant by the classroom window and the teacher said it needs sun to grow. Why do plants need sunlight?

response.1:
Great question — plants really do need sunlight! Here’s why, in a simple way:

- Sunlight is like food for plants. Plants use sunlight to make their own food in a process called photosynthesis. That’s a big word, but it just means “making food with light.”
- Inside the leaves are tiny helpers (chlorophyll) that are green. They catch sunlight and use it to turn water (from the soil) and carbon dioxide (a gas in the air) into sugar. The sugar is what the plant uses to grow and stay healthy.
- Sunlight also helps plants make oxygen. When plants do photosynthesis they release oxygen into the air — that’s the air we and animals breathe!
- If a plant doesn’t get enough sun, it may grow tall and thin while trying to reach the light, its leaves may turn pale, and it won’t grow very well.

An easy way to see this: put one small potted plant in a sunny window and one in a dark corner for a few weeks. The sunny one will look healthier and bushier.

If you want, you can help your classroom plant:
- Turn it a little every few days so all sides get sunlight.
- Make sure its soil is not too dry or too wet.
- Tell your teacher if the leaves look pale or droopy.

Would you like a simple experiment you can do with your class to watch photosynthesis?

prompt: My clock makes a tick-tock sound at night and I can hear it when I’m trying to sleep. Why do clocks tick?

response.1:
Good question — that tick-tock can be annoying when you want to sleep!

Why clocks tick
- Many clocks have moving parts inside called gears and a thing that swings back and forth (like a tiny seesaw). Each time the part swings one way and then the other, it makes a small click sound. That’s the “tick” and the “tock.”
- Old-fashioned wall clocks and some alarm clocks use a part called an escapement and a swinging piece called a pendulum or balance wheel. The escapement lets the gears move forward a little bit at a time. Each little step makes the tick-tock.
- Even some small battery clocks make a softer tick when the tiny motor moves the hands.

A simple example
- Think of a toy car with gears: when you push it, the gears turn in small steps and sometimes you can hear it click. A clock is like a very careful toy that measures time by those little clicks.

If the sound bothers you
- Move the clock to another room or across the room so the sound is quieter.
- Put the clock on soft material (like a folded cloth) — that can stop it from making a loud click on the table.
- Use a quieter clock (many digital clocks don’t tick) or try a small fan or a white-noise app to help you sleep.

If the ticking suddenly gets louder or strange, you can ask an adult (mum, dad, auntie, uncle, teacher) to check the clock — it might need new batteries or a small fix.

prompt: My mom says I can’t just run outside in my pajamas. Why do we wear clothes?

response.1:
That’s a good question — and lots of kids wonder the same thing.

We wear clothes for a few simple reasons kids can understand:

- To keep warm or cool. Clothes help our bodies stay the right temperature. If it’s cold, a jacket keeps you warm. If it’s hot, light clothes help you stay cool.
- To protect our skin. Clothes stop cuts, scrapes, sunburn, and insect bites when we play outside.
- For privacy and respect. Clothes cover parts of our bodies that are private. At home some people feel okay in pajamas, but when we go outside where other people are, it’s polite and respectful to wear normal clothes.
- For safety and rules. Schools, shops, and many places expect people to wear clothes. Grown-ups set rules so everyone is comfortable and safe.
- For fun and identity. Clothes can show what you like (a football shirt, a dress with animals) or help you fit into places like school or church.

If you want to run outside in your pajamas, you could ask your mom:
- “Can I change into something quick and still be warm?” or
- “Can I wear my pajamas in the yard for a bit?” 

That way you show you respect her rule but also explain what you want. If she says no, try suggesting a quick compromise like putting on a sweater or regular shorts over your pajamas.

prompt: At my friend’s birthday party we sang and ate cake and gave presents. Why do we celebrate birthdays every year?

response.1:
That sounds like a fun party!

We celebrate birthdays every year for a few simple reasons:

- To mark how much someone has grown. Each birthday tells us the person is one year older — taller, smarter, or a bit more independent than before.
- To say “you matter.” Birthday parties and cards show the person is loved and important to family and friends.
- To remember the day someone was born. It helps families keep stories and memories about that person alive.
- To make happy traditions. Singing, cake, games, and presents are ways people enjoy being together and make nice memories.

Different people and families do birthday things in their own way. Some have big parties, some pray at mosque or church, some share a special meal at home, and some keep it small. All of those ways are ways of celebrating the person.

If you want, you can think of one thing that makes your birthday special every year — a favourite game, a story, or someone you always like to see.

prompt: In my class some kids speak another language at home and their parents sound different on the phone. Why do people have different languages?

response.1:
That’s a great question — and a very curious thing to notice!

- People have different languages because long ago groups of people lived in different places and made their own words, sounds and ways of speaking. Over time those words changed, so one group’s language became different from another’s. It’s a bit like how cousins in different towns might start using different words for the same thing.

- Languages also change because of where people live, who they trade with, what jobs they do, and the stories and songs they share. If a family comes from a different state, town or country, they might speak the language or dialect they learned at home.

- Phones can make voices sound a little different too (quiet, loud, far away), and people sometimes use special words with their family that they don’t use at school.

- Having different languages is normal and good. It means we have lots of ways to say things, different songs, poems and stories. If you’re curious, you can politely ask a classmate, “How do you say ___ in your language?” Most children are happy to teach a word or two.

If you ever feel unsure about asking, you can talk to your teacher, auntie, uncle, or parent — they can help you learn more in a respectful way.
